title: Gold, weapons or a 'Rosetta stone': Which archaeological treasure would you most like to discover?
summary: From ancient coins to long-lost texts, archaeologists uncovered countless artifacts for centuries. Live Science asks its readers which one they'd want to discover themselves.
body: Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins , some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought , governed and died thousands of years ago. Related stories 'Links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial': How DNA solved the 70-year mystery of what happened to the executed members of the last Russian imperial family Ghostly 'sand body' double burial unearthed at Sutton Hoo 2,600-year-old inscription in Turkey finally deciphered — and it mentions goddess known 'simply as the Mother' Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. title: Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot: A 1,600-year-old silver and gold pepper shaker that a UK farmer unearthed while looking for his hammer
summary: This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.
body: The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard. (Image credit: Alamy) QUICK FACTS Name: Hoxne 'Empress' pepper pot What it is: A silver spice dispenser Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England When it was made: A.D. 350 to 400 In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady. The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum . The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.
